children.title: Bound-Tightening Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Variation in relaxation quality as variable bounds are refined.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Tightening Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies monotone improvement in a scalar RLT square relaxation under symmetric bound tightening.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the lifted scalar square model with \(-M\leq x\leq M\), the bound-product relaxation implies
\[w\geq\max\{2Mx-M^2,-2Mx-M^2\}=2M|x|-M^2.\]
At a fixed feasible value \(x=0\), its best lower estimate of \(x^2\) is \(-M^2\). Tightening the valid symmetric bound from radius \(M_1\) to \(M_2\), where \(0<M_2<M_1\), increases this relaxation lower bound from \(-M_1^2\) to \(-M_2^2\) and reduces the additive gap by \(M_1^2-M_2^2\). Hence bound quality directly controls this RLT gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the scalar square relaxation, shrinking a symmetric bound radius from M1 to M2 reduces the gap by the difference of their squares.
assumptions_latex: \(0<M_2<M_1\) and both intervals are valid bounds for the imposed point \(x=0\).

notation.meaning: Additive relaxation gap at x equal to zero under radius M.
Old and tightened symmetric bound radii.

children.title: Bound-Induced Unboundedness
children.top_down_role: Cases where insufficient domain information prevents preservation of a finite relaxation bound.

assumptions_latex: The original quadratic feasible set \(F\) is nonempty and has a finite optimal value.
The lifted relaxation is \(R=\{z:Az=b,\ z\in K\}\), with objective \(c^{\mathsf T}z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\operatorname{rec}(R)\) contains \(d\) with \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\), then the relaxation is unbounded below although the original problem has finite value.
review_flags: bound-specific formulation should be checked against the cited relaxation treatment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession-direction criterion for an unbounded lifted relaxation produced by inadequate variable-bound control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be the feasible set of a minimization problem with finite optimum, and let \(R\) be a lifted relaxation obtained using variable-bound inequalities. If there exist \(z_0\in R\) and a nonzero direction \(d\in\operatorname{rec}(R)\) such that \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\), then \(z_0+td\in R\) for every \(t\ge 0\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}(z_0+td)\to-\infty\). Thus the relaxation has value \(-\infty\), even though the original problem is bounded. This failure occurs when the imposed bounds and associated lifted inequalities do not eliminate an improving recession direction that has no counterpart in \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded quadratic problem can have an unbounded lifted relaxation when its bound-derived constraints leave an improving recession direction in the extended variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Bound-Induced Unboundedness

children.title: Independent-Product Inconsistency
children.top_down_role: Weakness caused by treating shared lifted products independently.

assumptions_latex: The shared variables satisfy \(0\le x\le1\) and \(0\le y\le1\).
Each lifted copy is constrained only by its own McCormick envelope for \(xy\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Separate envelope membership does not imply \(w_1=w_2=xy\); hence independently modeled copies can represent mutually inconsistent product values.

notation.meaning: Independent lifted copies intended to represent the same product.
McCormick envelope over the unit box.

review_flags: exact duplicated-product example requires source confirmation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete McCormick-envelope inconsistency for duplicated representations of one bilinear product.

source_refs.locator: 3.8 The GOP for Quadratic Problems with Linear Constraints p. 95

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0\le x,y\le1\), the McCormick envelope is \(M(x,y)=\{w:w\ge0,\ w\ge x+y-1,\ w\le x,\ w\le y\}\). Suppose two occurrences of the same product \(xy\) are replaced independently by \(w_1\) and \(w_2\), imposing only \(w_i\in M(x,y)\) for \(i\in\{1,2\}\). At \(x=y=\tfrac12\), both \(w_1=0\) and \(w_2=\tfrac12\) satisfy their respective envelopes. Nevertheless, no original point with these shared values can satisfy simultaneously \(w_1=xy\) and \(w_2=xy\). Omitting the linking equation \(w_1=w_2\) therefore strictly enlarges the relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two lifted copies of the same bilinear product may each satisfy a McCormick envelope while taking incompatible values unless an equality links them.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Product Inconsistency

children.title: Equivalent-Formulation Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Different bounds arising from algebraically equivalent quadratic models.

assumptions_latex: Two quadratic formulations have the same feasible original-variable set and identical objective values there.
A relaxation operator replaces or convexifies quadratic expressions according to their displayed algebraic occurrences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Algebraic equivalence of the original formulations does not guarantee equality of their relaxation bounds.

notation.meaning: Optimal value of a minimization formulation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noninvariance of termwise quadratic relaxations under equivalent algebraic reformulation.

source_refs.locator: 3.8 The GOP for Quadratic Problems with Linear Constraints p. 95

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_1\) and \(P_2\) be quadratic minimization formulations such that their projections onto the original variables coincide and their objectives agree at every original feasible point. Let \(\mathcal R(P_i)\) be relaxations constructed from the displayed quadratic terms, auxiliary variables, and available bounds in formulation \(P_i\). Equivalent-formulation sensitivity occurs when \(v(P_1)=v(P_2)\) but \(v(\mathcal R(P_1))\ne v(\mathcal R(P_2))\). In particular, rewriting a quadratic identity, duplicating a product variable, or adding a redundant quadratic equality can change the lifted constraints generated by \(\mathcal R\). Therefore equivalence before relaxation alone does not establish equivalence or equal strength after relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quadratic models with identical feasible points and objectives can yield different relaxation bounds because lifting and convexification depend on the displayed formulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent-Formulation Sensitivity

children.title: Conic Conditioning Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Weak feasibility margins, degeneracy, ill-conditioning, and scaling problems in conic relaxations.

children.title: Conic Feasibility Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Weak feasibility margins and deficient interior geometry in conic relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Feasibility Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of relative Slater feasibility and a sufficient proper-face certificate for a finite-dimensional conic system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a nonempty closed convex cone, let \(A:E\to Y\) be linear, and let \(b\in Y\). For the nonempty feasible set \(F=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\), conic feasibility degeneracy means \(F\cap\operatorname{ri}(K)=\varnothing\). A sufficient facial certificate is a vector \(y\in Y\) such that \(s=A^*y\in K^*\setminus\{0\}\), \(\langle b,y\rangle=0\), and \(K\cap s^\perp\subsetneq K\). Under these conditions, \(F\subseteq K\cap s^\perp\), so every feasible point lies in a proper exposed face of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible conic system is degenerate when it has no feasible point in the relative interior of its cone. A dual exposing vector certifies this when it places every feasible point in a proper exposed face.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real inner-product spaces.
\(K\subseteq E\) is a nonempty closed convex cone, \(A:E\to Y\) is linear, and \(b\in Y\).
The feasible set \(F=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(y\in Y\) satisfies \(A^*y\in K^*\setminus\{0\}\), \(\langle b,y\rangle=0\), and \(K\cap(A^*y)^\perp\subsetneq K\), then \(F\) lies in that proper exposed face and has no point in \(\operatorname{ri}(K)\).

notation.meaning: Nonempty closed convex cone in E.
Adjoint of the linear map A.

review_flags: facial certificate should be confirmed against a dedicated conic or facial-reduction source

children.title: Conic Ill-Conditioning
children.top_down_role: Numerical sensitivity arising from poorly conditioned conic representations.

assumptions_latex: Conic data \(d=(A,b,c)\) are measured in a fixed norm.
The distance \(\rho(d)\) is taken to the nearest data instance with a changed primal-dual feasibility status.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Small positive \(\rho(d)\) gives a large condition number, while \(\rho(d)=0\) marks ill-posed conic data.

notation.meaning: Distance from the data to ill-posedness.

review_flags: the cited section may not contain the stated distance-to-ill-posedness convention
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normwise distance-to-ill-posedness definition for finite-dimensional conic programs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For conic data \(d=(A,b,c)\), let \(\Sigma\) denote the boundary between data having stable primal-dual feasibility status and data having a different status, and define \(\rho(d)=\inf_{\tilde d\in\Sigma}\|d-\tilde d\|\). When \(\rho(d)>0\), define the relative condition number by \(\kappa(d)=\|d\|/\rho(d)\). The conic formulation is ill-conditioned when \(\kappa(d)\) is large: perturbations small relative to \(\|d\|\) can then substantially alter feasibility certificates, solutions, or optimal values. If \(\rho(d)=0\), set \(\kappa(d)=+\infty\); the data are ill-posed under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conic data are ill-conditioned when they lie close, relative to their norm, to data where primal-dual feasibility status changes.
knowledge_statements.title: Conic Ill-Conditioning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited general conic-programming section does not establish this distance-to-ill-posedness convention. The set separating feasibility statuses and the primal-dual status partition are insufficiently defined, while conclusions about solutions and optimal values exceed the stated feasibility-distance definition. A dedicated source for a specific conic condition number is required.

children.title: Conic Scaling Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Bound and solver degradation caused by incompatible coefficient scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Conic Scaling Pathologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Numerical noninvariance of equivalent finite-dimensional conic formulations under row and cone-preserving variable scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional normed spaces, let \(K\subseteq E\) be a closed convex cone, and consider \(\min\{\langle c,x\rangle:Ax=b,\ x\in K\}\). Let \(D:Y\to Y\) be invertible and let \(S:E\to E\) be invertible with \(S(K)=K\). Under \(x=Sz\), the equivalent scaled formulation is \(DASz=Db\), \(z\in K\), with objective \(\langle S^*c,z\rangle\). Exact feasible points and optimal solutions correspond bijectively, but the primal residual satisfies \(r'_p(z)=D(Ax-b)=Dr_p(x)\). Thus absolute residual norms, coefficient magnitudes, and unadjusted norm-based stopping tests are not invariant under scaling and can be severely distorted by extreme choices of \(D\) or \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invertible row and cone-preserving variable scalings leave the exact conic problem equivalent, but they can severely distort residual norms, coefficient magnitudes, and stopping tests that are not transformed consistently.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces, \(K\subseteq E\) is a closed convex cone, \(A:E\to Y\) is linear, \(b\in Y\), and \(c\in E^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scaled and unscaled conic programs are exactly equivalent, while \(r'_p=Dr_p\); consequently, numerical quantities based on unadjusted coefficient or residual norms need not be invariant.

notation.meaning: Invertible cone automorphism used for variable scaling.
Primal equation residual in the original formulation.
Primal equation residual in the scaled formulation.

children.title: Degeneracy–Scaling Interaction
children.top_down_role: Regimes where poor scaling amplifies geometric degeneracy or weak feasibility margins.

assumptions_latex: The feasible conic system \(Ax=b\), \(x\in K\), has no point in \(\operatorname{ri}(K)\).
The scaling uses invertible \(D\) and a cone automorphism \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scaling cannot remove facial degeneracy, although poorly conditioned scaling can magnify its numerical effects.
review_flags: interaction with numerical residuals requires a dedicated conic-analysis source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariance of Slater failure and amplification of numerical symptoms under scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{x\in K:Ax=b\}\) satisfy \(F\cap\operatorname{ri}(K)=\varnothing\). Under \(x=Sz\), where \(S\) is a cone automorphism, the transformed feasible set is \(S^{-1}F\). Since \(S^{-1}\operatorname{ri}(K)=\operatorname{ri}(K)\), one has \(S^{-1}F\cap\operatorname{ri}(K)=\varnothing\); hence invertible scaling cannot restore Slater feasibility or remove containment in a proper face. Nevertheless, row or variable scalings with large normwise condition numbers can amplify residuals associated with the exposing face and obscure numerical detection of degeneracy. Thus degeneracy is geometrically invariant while its observed numerical severity is scaling dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone-preserving scaling cannot cure missing strict feasibility, but extreme scaling can amplify residuals and make the underlying facial degeneracy harder to detect.
knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy–Scaling Interaction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The geometric invariance of relative Slater failure under a cone automorphism is standard and precise. However, the claims about amplification of exposing-face residuals, observed severity, and obscured detection do not define the residuals or numerical procedure and are not supported by the cited general conic-programming locator. A dedicated numerical conic-analysis source is required.

children.title: Recovery without Feasibility Preservation
children.top_down_role: Failure of rounded or extracted vectors to preserve quadratic or combinatorial feasibility.

assumptions_latex: A semidefinite relaxation returns \(X\succeq0\) for constraints originally imposed on \(xx^{\mathsf T}\).
Recovery selects a vector from one rank-one component without a feasibility-preserving correction step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility of \(X\) does not imply feasibility of an extracted vector when \(\operatorname{rank}(X)>1\).
review_flags: specific extraction counterexample requires source confirmation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-one extraction from a feasible semidefinite relaxation need not preserve original quadratic equalities.

source_refs.locator: 5. Approximation Algorithms in Quadratic Programming p. 38

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider original variables \(x\in\mathbb R^2\) subject to \(x_1^2=x_2^2=1\). The lifted semidefinite constraints \(X\succeq0\) and \(X_{11}=X_{22}=1\) admit \(X=I_2\), which has rank two and is not equal to \(xx^{\mathsf T}\) for any feasible \(x\). A leading-eigenvector extraction may choose \(\hat x=e_1\), because \(e_1\) is a unit eigenvector of \(I_2\). This recovered vector satisfies \(\hat x_1^2=1\) but violates \(\hat x_2^2=1\). Therefore lifted feasibility alone does not make such an extraction map feasibility preserving; repair, projection, or specialized rounding is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible higher-rank semidefinite matrix can yield an extracted vector that violates the original quadratic constraints, even when the matrix satisfies every lifted constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Recovery without Feasibility Preservation

source_witnesses.locator: 5. Approximation Algorithms in Quadratic Programming p. 38
